title: Bystanders and a dropped bag of groceries

readings.title: Invented study: Does the number of bystanders change helping?
readings.html:
Introduction

The bystander effect predicts that each person is less likely to help when other people are present, partly through diffusion of responsibility. Researchers tested this in a staged, everyday situation. Hypothesis: participants waiting alone would help more often and more quickly than participants waiting with other people.

Participants

120 students at a community college in Arizona (ages 18 to 34; 66 women and 54 men; 52% Hispanic, 31% White, 9% Native American, 8% other) signed up for what they were told was a study of reading speed. The college's institutional review board approved the study, including its use of deception.

Method

Participants were randomly assigned to wait for the "reading study" in a hallway alone, with 1 other person or with 4 other people. The others were confederates who had been told to keep reading their phones. After 2 minutes, a different confederate walked past carrying a grocery bag, which split open, and fruit rolled across the floor. Helping was recorded as the participant picking up at least one item or asking whether the person needed help, within 60 seconds of the bag splitting. A hidden observer, who did not know the hypothesis, also recorded the seconds until helping began. Afterward, each participant was debriefed: told that the reading study and the bag were staged, why deception was needed, and that they could have their data removed. Two participants asked for this, and their data were removed and replaced.

Results

The percent of participants who helped within 60 seconds was 78% when alone, 55% with 1 other person and 33% with 4 other people. Among those who helped, mean time to help was 6 seconds alone, 11 seconds with 1 other and 17 seconds with 4 others. The difference in the percent who helped between the alone and 4-other conditions was statistically significant.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that helping fell as the number of bystanders rose. They noted that a dropped bag is a minor event and that results may differ in serious emergencies.

Invented study for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.point: Identifies the method as an experiment
accept: an experiment with random assignment to three conditions

parts.sample: This study is an experiment, because the researchers manipulated the number of people waiting with the participant (none, 1 or 4) and randomly assigned participants to those conditions.

parts.label: B

rubric.point: States helping as picking up at least one item or asking whether the person needed help, within 60 seconds of the bag splitting
accept: picking up fruit or offering help within 60 seconds
whether the participant picked up an item or asked if the person needed help within one minute

parts.sample: Helping was defined as the participant picking up at least one piece of fallen fruit or asking the person whether they needed help, within 60 seconds after the bag split.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Describe what the percent who helped in the alone condition, compared with the 4-other condition, shows.

rubric.point: Says more than twice as many participants helped when alone (78%) as with 4 others (33%), and that because the difference was statistically significant it is unlikely to be due to chance
accept: participants were much more likely to help when no one else was there, a difference unlikely to be due to chance

parts.sample: 78% of participants who waited alone helped, compared with only 33% of those who waited with 4 others, so people alone were more than twice as likely to help. Because this difference was statistically significant, it is unlikely to be due to chance and is probably caused by the number of bystanders.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline the researchers followed, and explain how they applied it in this study.

rubric.point: Names a safeguard the summary describes and how it was applied: debriefing after deception (told the reading study and bag were staged and why), IRB approval of the deception, or the option to remove one's data (two did, and their data were removed)
accept: debriefing: participants were told afterward the bag accident was staged and why deception was needed
IRB approval: the college review board approved the study and its deception
participants could have their data removed after learning the truth, and two did

parts.sample: The researchers debriefed participants. Because participants were deceived about the reading study and the bag accident, afterward the researchers told each one that both were staged, explained why the deception was needed, and offered to remove their data.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable using specific and relevant evidence from the study.

rubric.point: Makes a claim about generalizing to a named population, supported by participant characteristics
accept: generalizes to young adults in the US Southwest, since participants were 18 to 34, men and women, of several ethnic groups
may not generalize to older adults or children, since all participants were 18 to 34 college students
partly: a varied group by gender and ethnicity, but all from one community college

parts.sample: The findings may generalize to young adult college students in the southwestern United States, because participants were 18 to 34, both women and men, and from several ethnic groups. They may not generalize to older adults or children, because no participant was younger than 18 or older than 34.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the researchers' hypothesis that participants waiting alone would help more often and more quickly than participants waiting with others.

rubric.point: Uses a specific, accurate result from the study
accept: helping fell from 78% alone to 55% with 1 other to 33% with 4 others
mean time to help rose from 6 to 11 to 17 seconds

rubric.point: Explains how the result supports the hypothesis
accept: people alone helped more often and faster, as predicted by diffusion of responsibility

parts.sample: The findings support the hypothesis. Participants alone helped more often (78%) than those with 1 other (55%) or 4 others (33%), and among helpers they helped faster: 6 seconds alone against 17 seconds with 4 others. With others present, each person could assume someone else would act (diffusion of responsibility), so helping was both less likely and slower, exactly as the hypothesis predicted.
